# ankurah - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ankurah/0.8.1/ankurah/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ankurah)Ankurah

Ankurah is a state-management framework that enables real-time data synchronization across multiple nodes with built-in observability.

It supports multiple storage and data type backends to enable no-compromise representation of your data.

This project is in the early stages of development, and is not yet ready for production use.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-features)Key Features

- **Schema-First Design**: Define data models using Rust structs with an ActiveRecord-style interface -- [View](https://docs.rs/trait.Model.html#associatedtype.View)/- [Mutable](https://docs.rs/trait.Model.html#associatedtype.Mutable)
- **Content-filtered pub/sub**: Subscribe to changes on a collection using a SQL-like query -- [subscribe](Node::subscribe)
- **Real-Time Observability**: Signal-based pattern for tracking entity changes
- **Distributed Architecture**: Multi-node synchronization with event sourcing
- **Flexible Storage**: Support for multiple storage backends (Sled, Postgres, TiKV)
- **Isomorphic code**: Server applications and Web applications use the same code, including first-class support for React and Leptos out of the box

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

- **Model**: A struct describing fields and types for entities in a collection (data binding)
- **Collection**: A group of entities of the same type (similar to a database table, and backed by a table in the postgres backend)
- **Entity**: A discrete identity in a collection - Dynamic schema (similar to a schema-less database row)
- **View**: A read-only representation of an entity - Typed by the model
- **Mutable**: A mutable state representation of an entity - Typed by the model
- **Event**: An atomic change that can be applied to an entity - used for syncrhonization and audit trail

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

- Start the server:

```
cargo run -p ankurah-example-server
# or dev mode
cargo watch -x 'run -p ankurah-example-server'
```
- Build WASM bindings:

```
cd examples/wasm-bindings
wasm-pack build --target web --debug
# or dev mode
cargo watch -s 'wasm-pack build --target web --debug'
```
- Run the React example app:

```
cd examples/react-app
bun install
bun dev
```
Then load http://localhost:5173/ in one regular browser tab, and one incognito browser tab and play with the example app. You can also use two regular browser tabs, but they share one IndexedDB local storage backend, so it’s not as good of a test. In this example, the “server” process is a native Rust process whose node is flagged as “durable”, meaning that it attests it will not lose data. The “client” process is a WASM process that is also durable in some sense, but not to be relied upon to have all data. The demo server currently uses the sled backend, but postgres is also supported, and TiKV support is planned.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-inter-node-subscription)Example: Inter-Node Subscription

```
#[derive(Model, Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Album {
    name: String,
    year: String,
}
    // Create server and client nodes
    let server = Node::new_durable(Arc::new(SledStorageEngine::new_test()?), ankurah::policy::PermissiveAgent::new());
    server.system.create().await?;
    let client = Node::new(Arc::new(SledStorageEngine::new_test()?), ankurah::policy::PermissiveAgent::new());
    // Connect nodes using local process connection
    let _conn = LocalProcessConnection::new(&server, &client).await?;
    client.system.wait_system_ready().await; // Wait for the client to join the server "system"
    // Get contexts for the server and client
    let server = server.context(ankurah::policy::DEFAULT_CONTEXT)?;
    let client = client.context(ankurah::policy::DEFAULT_CONTEXT)?;
    // Create a LiveQuery and subscribe to changes on the client
    let livequery = client.query::<AlbumView>("name = 'Origin of Symmetry'")?;
    use ankurah::signals::Subscribe;
    let _guard = livequery.subscribe(|changes| {
        println!("Received changes: {}", changes);
    });
    // Create a new album on the server
    let trx = server.begin();
    trx.create(&Album {
        name: "Origin of Symmetry".into(),
        year: "2001".into(),
    }).await;
    trx.commit().await?;
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-philosophy)Design Philosophy

Ankurah follows an event-sourced architecture where:

- All operations have unique IDs and precursor operations
- Entity state is maintained per node with operation tree tracking
- Operations use ULID for distributed ID generation
- Entity IDs are derived from their creation operation

For more details, see the [repository documentation](https://github.com/ankurah/ankurah).
And join the [Discord server](https://discord.gg/XMUUxsbT5S) to be part of the discussion!

# ankurah_signals - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ankurah-signals/0.8.1/ankurah_signals/

## Expand description

A signals library designed to support Ankurah’s needs - but can be used independently as well. Supports both native Rust and WebAssembly/React use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-in-rust)Basic Usage in Rust

```
let day = Mut::new("Friday");
let vibe = Mut::new("grindcore");
// Sometimes directly subscribing to the signal can be useful
// your listener will not be called immediately, only when the signal changes
// the subscription will be removed when the SubscriptionGuard is dropped
let _guard1 = day.subscribe(|v| println!("The day is: {}", v));
let _guard2 = vibe.subscribe(|v| println!("Vibe: {}", v));
// For things that need to track signal dependencies, we can use an Observer
let renderer = {
    let day = day.read(); // Read<T> signals can be constructed from a Mut<T> signal
    let vibe = vibe.read();
    CallbackObserver::new(Arc::new(move ||{
        // Your "render" function that uses signals
        // The Observer will automatically subscribe to the signals used
        // during this dispatch using the thread-local CurrentObserver
        println!("It's {day} and I'm {vibe}") // the Observer will automatically subscribe to the signals
    }))
};
renderer.trigger(); // trigger the initial "render". Signals used will be tracked by the observer.
// Should print:
// It's Friday and I'm grindcore
vibe.set("chillmaxing"); // triggers the direct signal subscription AND the observer
// Should print:
// Vibe: chillmaxing
// It's Friday and I'm chillmaxing
day.set("Saturday");
// Should print:
// The day is: Saturday
// It's Saturday and I'm chillmaxing
```

# cpal 0.18.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpal/0.18.1

# CPAL - Cross-Platform Audio Library

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider [Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

## Supported Functionality

- Enumerate audio hosts, devices, and their supported stream configurations.
- Look up devices by stable ID or by default input/output role.
- Inspect device metadata: name, manufacturer, type, and bus type.
- Build input and output streams with compile-time or runtime sample formats.
- Play, pause, and query the buffer size and clock of a stream.

## Supported Platforms

| Platform | Default Backend | Optional Backends |
|---|---|---|
| Android | AAudio | - |
| BSD | ALSA | JACK, PipeWire, PulseAudio |
| iOS | CoreAudio | - |
| Linux | ALSA | JACK, PipeWire, PulseAudio |
| macOS | CoreAudio | JACK |
| tvOS | CoreAudio | - |
| WebAssembly | Web Audio API | Audio Worklet |
| Windows | WASAPI | ASIO, JACK |

## Linux Build Dependencies

On Linux, building cpal requires the ALSA development files: `libasound2-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu, `alsa-lib-devel` on Fedora.

ALSA is needed even when using JACK, PipeWire, or PulseAudio.

The optional `realtime-dbus` feature additionally requires `libdbus-1-dev` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `dbus-devel` (Fedora). See [ALSA Real-Time Priority Promotion](https://docs.rs#alsa-real-time-priority-promotion).

## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

The minimum Rust version required depends on which audio backend and features you're using, as each platform has different dependencies:

| Backend | Platforms | MSRV |
|---|---|---|
| AAudio | Android | 1.85 |
| ALSA | Linux, BSD | 1.85 |
| CoreAudio | macOS, iOS | 1.85 |
| CoreAudio | tvOS | nightly |
| JACK | Linux, BSD, macOS, Windows | 1.85 |
| PipeWire | Linux, BSD | 1.85 |
| PulseAudio | Linux, BSD | 1.88 |
| WASAPI / ASIO | Windows | 1.85 |
| WASM ( `wasm32-unknown`) | WebAssembly | 1.85 |
| WASM ( `wasm32-wasip1`) | WebAssembly | 1.85 |
| WASM ( `audioworklet`) | WebAssembly | nightly |

The `audioworklet` backend additionally requires `-Zbuild-std` with atomics support enabled.

## Optional Features

| Feature | Platform | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `asio` | Windows | ASIO backend for low-latency audio, bypassing the Windows audio stack. Requires ASIO drivers and LLVM/Clang. See the [ASIO setup guide](https://docs.rs#compiling-for-asio). |
| `audioworklet` | WebAssembly ( `wasm32-unknown-unknown`) | Audio Worklet backend for lower-latency web audio than the default Web Audio API, running audio on a dedicated thread. Requires atomics support ( `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+atomics,+bulk-memory,+mutable-globals"`) and`Cross-Origin`headers for`SharedArrayBuffer`. See the`audioworklet-beep`example. |
| `custom` | All | User-defined backend implementations for audio systems not natively supported by CPAL. See `examples/custom.rs`. |
| `jack` | Linux, BSD, macOS, Windows | JACK Audio Connection Kit backend for pro-audio routing and inter-application connectivity. Requires `libjack-jackd2-dev`(Debian/Ubuntu) or`jack-devel`(Fedora). |
| `pipewire` | Linux, BSD | PipeWire media server backend. Requires `libpipewire-0.3-dev`(Debian/Ubuntu) or`pipewire-devel`(Fedora). |
| `pulseaudio` | Linux, BSD | PulseAudio sound server backend. Requires `libpulse-dev`(Debian/Ubuntu) or`pulseaudio-libs-devel`(Fedora). |
| `realtime` | Linux, BSD, Windows, Android | Raises the audio callback thread to real-time or high-priority scheduling for lower latency. On Linux/BSD, requires `rtprio`granted in`limits.conf`(e.g.`@audio - rtprio 95`) unless`realtime-dbus`is also enabled. |
| `realtime-dbus` | Linux, BSD | Uses `rtkit`via D-Bus for RT scheduling on Linux/BSD desktop systems, removing the need for manual`limits.conf`setup. Implies`realtime`on all platforms. Requires`libdbus-1-dev`on Linux/BSD. |
| `wasm-bindgen` | WebAssembly ( `wasm32-unknown-unknown`) | Web Audio API backend for browser-based audio; required for any WebAssembly audio support. See the `wasm-beep`example. |

See the [beep example](https://docs.rs/examples/beep.rs) for selecting the backend at runtime.

## Compiling for ASIO

### Locating the ASIO SDK

The location of ASIO SDK is exposed to CPAL by setting the `CPAL_ASIO_DIR` environment variable.

The build script will try to find the ASIO SDK by following these steps in order:

- Check if `CPAL_ASIO_DIR`is set and if so use the path to point to the SDK.
- Check if the ASIO SDK is already installed in the temporary directory, if so use that and set the path of `CPAL_ASIO_DIR`to the output of`std::env::temp_dir().join("asio_sdk")`.
- If the ASIO SDK is not already installed, download it from [https://www.steinberg.net/asiosdk](https://www.steinberg.net/asiosdk)and install it in the temporary directory. The path of`CPAL_ASIO_DIR`will be set to the output of`std::env::temp_dir().join("asio_sdk")`.

In an ideal situation you don't need to worry about this step.

### Preparing the Build Environment

-
**Install LLVM/Clang**:`bindgen`, the library used to generate bindings to the C++ SDK, requires clang. Download and install LLVM from[http://releases.llvm.org/download.html](http://releases.llvm.org/download.html)under the "Pre-Built Binaries" section.
-
**Set LIBCLANG_PATH**: Add the LLVM`bin`directory to a`LIBCLANG_PATH`environment variable. If you installed LLVM to the default directory, this should work in the command prompt:`setx LIBCLANG_PATH "C:\Program Files\LLVM\bin"`
-
**Install ASIO Drivers**(optional for testing): If you don't have any ASIO devices or drivers available, you can download and install ASIO4ALL from[http://www.asio4all.org/](http://www.asio4all.org/). Be sure to enable the "offline" feature during installation.
-
**Visual Studio**: The build script assumes Microsoft Visual Studio is installed. It will try to find`vcvarsall.bat`and execute it with the right host and target architecture. If needed, you can manually execute it:`"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2019\Community\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvarsall.bat" amd64`For more information see the [vcvarsall.bat documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/building-on-the-command-line).

### Using ASIO in Your Application

-
**Enable the feature**in your`Cargo.toml`:`= { = "*", = ["asio"] }`
-
**Select the ASIO backend**in your code:`let host = host_from_id .expect;`

### Cross-Compilation

When Windows is the host and target OS, the build script supports all cross-compilation targets supported by the MSVC compiler.

It is also possible to compile Windows applications with ASIO support on Linux and macOS using the MinGW-w64 toolchain.

**Requirements:**

- Include the MinGW-w64 include directory in your `CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH`environment variable
- Include the LLVM include directory in your `CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH`environment variable

**Example for macOS** (targeting `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` with `mingw-w64` installed via brew):

```
```
## Compiling for WebAssembly

If you are interested in using CPAL with WebAssembly, please see [this guide](https://github.com/RustAudio/cpal/wiki/Setting-up-a-new-CPAL-WASM-project) in our Wiki which walks through setting up a new project from scratch. Some of the examples in this repository also provide working configurations that you can use as reference.

## Troubleshooting

### No Default Device Available

If you receive errors about no default input or output device:

- **Linux/PipeWire:**Check that PipeWire is running:- `pw-cli info`
- **Linux/PulseAudio:**Check that PulseAudio is running:- `pulseaudio --check`
- **macOS:**Check System Preferences > Sound for available devices
- **Mobile (iOS/Android):**Ensure your app has microphone/audio permissions
- **Windows:**Verify your audio device is enabled in Sound Settings

## ALSA, PipeWire, and PulseAudio

When PipeWire or PulseAudio is running, it holds the ALSA `default` device exclusively. A second stream attempting to open it via the ALSA host will fail with a `DeviceBusy` error. To route audio through the sound server via ALSA, use the bridge devices `pipewire` or `pulse` instead of `default`. Better yet, use the `pipewire` or `pulseaudio` cpal features for native integration.

On targets without a sound server, address devices directly as `hw:` or `plughw:`.

### Buffer Size Issues

`BufferSize::Default` uses the system-configured device default, which on **ALSA** can range from a PipeWire quantum (typically 1024 frames) to `u32::MAX` on misconfigured or exotic hardware. A very deep buffer causes samples to be consumed far faster than audible playback, making audio appear to fast-forward ahead of actual output.

Configure the system and/or request a fixed size in your application:

| System | File | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| ALSA | `~/.asoundrc`or`/etc/asound.conf` | `buffer_size`,`periods`*`period_size` |
| PipeWire | `~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/` | `default.clock.quantum` |
| PulseAudio | `~/.config/pulse/daemon.conf` | `default-fragments`*`default-fragment-size-msec` |

```
config.buffer_size = Fixed;
```
Query `device.default_output_config()?.buffer_size()` for valid ranges. Smaller buffers reduce latency but increase CPU load and the risk of glitches.

### ALSA Real-Time Priority Promotion

RT promotion is only attempted for a whitelist of PCM types: direct hardware PCMs (`hw:`) and pure format-conversion plugins (linear, A-law, mu-law, ADPCM, float, IEC 958).

`RealtimeDenied` is emitted on the error callback only when promotion is attempted but fails, which happens when the process lacks the resource limits to acquire `SCHED_FIFO`. While RT priority is desirable for low latency, the stream will continue to play at the default scheduling priority.

With the `realtime-dbus` feature, `rtkit` arranges the necessary limits over D-Bus on typical desktop systems. With the plain `realtime` feature, you must ensure that `rtprio` is granted yourself. Add to `/etc/security/limits.d/audio.conf` and ensure the user is member of the `audio` group:

```
@audio - rtprio 95
```
then add the user to the `audio` group (`usermod -aG audio "$USER"`) and re-login. The same group may anyway be needed to grant access to ALSA device files via `udev` on systems that do not arrange this automatically via `logind`.

### Build Errors

If you are unable to build the library:

- Verify you have installed the required development libraries, as documented above
- **ASIO on Windows:**Verify- `CPAL_ASIO_DIR`and- `LIBCLANG_PATH`are set and LLVM is installed

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpal/0.18.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/cpal/

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescription](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescription.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescriptionBuilder](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescriptionBuilder.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDirection](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceDirection.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceType.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [InterfaceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.InterfaceType.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [available_hosts](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.available_hosts.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [host_from_id](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.host_from_id.html);

- 48 kHz: the EBU/SMPTE broadcast standard, default on most modern hardware.
- [SAMPLE_](https://docs.rs/constant.SAMPLE_RATE_CD.html)- RATE_ - CD
- 44.1 kHz: the CD standard, widely used in music production and consumer audio.

- Similar to the std `From`trait, but specifically for converting between sample types.

- [Channel](https://docs.rs/type.ChannelCount.html)- Count
- Number of channels.
- [Devices](https://docs.rs/type.DevicesFiltered.html)- Filtered
- Iterator of devices wrapped in a filter to only include certain device types
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html)- Count
- A frame represents one sample for each channel. For example, with stereo audio, one frame contains two samples (left and right channels).
- [Input](https://docs.rs/type.InputDevices.html)- Devices
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *input*devices.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/type.OutputDevices.html)- Devices
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *output*devices.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/type.SampleRate.html)- Rate
- The number of samples processed per second for a single channel of audio.

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpal/0.18.1/target-redirect/aarch64-linux-android/cpal/

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescription](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescription.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescriptionBuilder](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescriptionBuilder.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDirection](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceDirection.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceType.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [InterfaceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.InterfaceType.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [available_hosts](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.available_hosts.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [host_from_id](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.host_from_id.html);

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescriptionBuilder](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescriptionBuilder.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDirection](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceDirection.html);

    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/index.html

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

# lib.rs - source

# cpal/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! # How to use cpal
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! Here are some concepts cpal exposes:
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! - A [`Host`] provides access to the available audio devices on the system.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!   Some platforms have more than one host available, but every platform supported by CPAL has at
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!   least one [default_host] that is guaranteed to be available.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! - A [`Device`] is an audio device that may have any number of input and
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!   output streams.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! - A [`Stream`] is an open flow of audio data. Input streams allow you to
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!   receive audio data, output streams allow you to play audio data. You must choose which
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!   [Device] will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   retrieved via the [Host].
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! The first step is to initialise the [`Host`]:
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! ```
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! let host = cpal::default_host();
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! ```
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! Then choose an available [`Device`]. The easiest way is to use the default input or output
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! `Device` via the [`default_input_device()`] or [`default_output_device()`] methods on `host`.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [`devices()`] method.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! Beware that the `default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! is available for that stream type on the system.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```no_run
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! # use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! # let host = cpal::default_host();
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! ```
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! going to be.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! You can query all the supported configurations with the
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! [`supported_input_configs()`] and [`supported_output_configs()`] methods.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! These produce a list of [`SupportedStreamConfigRange`] structs which can later be turned into
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! actual [`SupportedStreamConfig`] structs.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! If you don't want to query the list of configs,
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! you can also build your own [`StreamConfig`] manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! > **Note**: the `supported_input/output_configs()` methods
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! > could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! ```no_run
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! # let host = cpal::default_host();
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! # let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!     .expect("error while querying configs");
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!     .expect("no supported config?!")
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     .with_max_sample_rate();
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! ```
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! ```no_run
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! use cpal::Data;
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! # let host = cpal::default_host();
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! # let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! # let config = device.default_output_config().unwrap().into();
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! let stream = device.build_output_stream(
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!     config,
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!         // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     },
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     move |err| {
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!         // react to errors here.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     },
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!          // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! );
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! [`Stream::play`](traits::StreamTrait::play), the selected audio device will periodically call
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! `&`[`Data`] containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! `&mut`[`Data`] to be filled with audio samples for playback.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! > **Note**: Creating and running a stream will *not* block the thread. On modern platforms, the
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! > given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! > audio data to the system's audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! > provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! > provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! > use a single thread for all streams). *If this is an issue for your platform or design,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! > please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! > consideration.*
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! ```no_run
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! # let host = cpal::default_host();
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! # let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! # let supported_config = device.default_output_config().unwrap();
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! let config = supported_config.into();
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! let stream = match sample_format {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!     SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!     SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!     SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!     sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! }.unwrap();
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     for sample in data.iter_mut() {
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!         *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     }
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! }
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! ```
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! [`Stream::play`](traits::StreamTrait::play) to start running the data callback.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! ```no_run
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! # let host = cpal::default_host();
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! # let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! # let supported_config = device.default_output_config().unwrap();
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! # let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! # let config = supported_config.into();
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! # let data_fn = move |_data: &mut cpal::Data, _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {};
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! # let err_fn = move |_err| {};
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! # let stream = device.build_output_stream_raw(config, sample_format, data_fn, err_fn, None).unwrap();
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! stream.play().unwrap();
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! of silence.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! ```no_run
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! # use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! # let host = cpal::default_host();
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! # let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! # let supported_config = device.default_output_config().unwrap();
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! # let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! # let config = supported_config.into();
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! # let data_fn = move |_data: &mut cpal::Data, _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {};
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! # let err_fn = move |_err| {};
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! # let stream = device.build_output_stream_raw(config, sample_format, data_fn, err_fn, None).unwrap();
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! stream.pause().unwrap();
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! ```
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! [`default_input_device()`]: traits::HostTrait::default_input_device
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! [`default_output_device()`]: traits::HostTrait::default_output_device
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! [`devices()`]: traits::HostTrait::devices
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! [`supported_input_configs()`]: traits::DeviceTrait::supported_input_configs
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! [`supported_output_configs()`]: traits::DeviceTrait::supported_output_configs

[235](https://docs.rs#235)/// A stable identifier for an audio device across all supported platforms.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)///
[237](https://docs.rs#237)/// Device IDs should remain stable across application restarts and can be serialized using `Display`/`FromStr`.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)///
[239](https://docs.rs#239)/// A device ID consists of a [`HostId`] identifying the audio backend and a device-specific identifier string.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)///
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// # Example
[242](https://docs.rs#242)///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// ```no_run
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// use cpal::traits::{HostTrait, DeviceTrait};
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// use cpal::DeviceId;
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// use std::str::FromStr;
[247](https://docs.rs#247)///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// let host = cpal::default_host();
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
[250](https://docs.rs#250)/// let device_id = device.id().unwrap();
[251](https://docs.rs#251)///
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// // Serialize to string (e.g., for storage in config file)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// let id_string = device_id.to_string();
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// println!("Device ID: {}", id_string); // e.g., "wasapi:device_identifier"
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// // Deserialize from string
[257](https://docs.rs#257)/// match DeviceId::from_str(&id_string) {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///     Ok(parsed_id) => {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)///         // Retrieve the device by its ID
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///         if let Some(device) = host.device_by_id(&parsed_id) {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)///             println!("Found device: {:?}", device.id());
[262](https://docs.rs#262)///         }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)///     }
[264](https://docs.rs#264)///     Err(e) => eprintln!("Failed to parse device ID: {}", e),
[265](https://docs.rs#265)/// }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)/// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
[268](https://docs.rs#268)pub struct DeviceId(crate::platform::HostId, Box<str>);
[269](https://docs.rs#269)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)impl DeviceId {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// Creates a `DeviceId` from a host identifier and a device-specific identifier string.
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ///
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// This constructor is used by backend implementations. Application code should obtain
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// `DeviceId` values through [`DeviceTrait::id`] and persist them via [`Display`]/[`FromStr`].
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// [`DeviceTrait::id`]: crate::traits::DeviceTrait::id
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// [`Display`]: std::fmt::Display
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// [`FromStr`]: std::str::FromStr
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    pub fn new(host: crate::platform::HostId, id: impl AsRef<str>) -> Self {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        Self(host, Box::from(id.as_ref()))
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    }
[282](https://docs.rs#282)
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    /// Returns the host this device belongs to.
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    pub fn host(&self) -> crate::platform::HostId {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        self.0
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// Returns the backend-specific device identifier string.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    pub fn id(&self) -> &str {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        &self.1
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)}
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)impl std::fmt::Display for DeviceId {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        write!(f, "{}:{}", self.host(), self.id())
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    }
[298](https://docs.rs#298)}
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)impl std::str::FromStr for DeviceId {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    type Err = Error;
[302](https://docs.rs#302)
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    /// Parse a device identifier from its string representation (e.g. `"alsa:hw:0,0"`).
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    ///
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// The format is `"<host>:<device>"` where `<host>` is the lowercase host name (see
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// [`HostId`]) and `<device>` is the device-specific identifier string.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    ///
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// # Errors
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    ///
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// - [`ErrorKind::InvalidInput`] if the string is not in `"host:device"` format.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// - [`ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation`] if the host portion names a host not available on this
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    ///   platform.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    ///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// [`ErrorKind::InvalidInput`]: ErrorKind::InvalidInput
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// [`ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation`]: ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        let (host_str, device_str) = s.split_once(':').ok_or_else(|| {
[318](https://docs.rs#318)            Error::with_message(
[319](https://docs.rs#319)                ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
[320](https://docs.rs#320)                format!("failed to parse device ID \"{s}\": expected \"host:device_id\" format"),
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            )
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        })?;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        let host_id = crate::platform::HostId::from_str(host_str)?;
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        Ok(Self::new(host_id, device_str))
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    }
[328](https://docs.rs#328)}
[329](https://docs.rs#329)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// The buffer size requests the callback size for audio streams.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)///
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// This controls the approximate size of the audio buffer passed to your callback.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)/// The actual callback size depends on the host/platform implementation and hardware
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// constraints, and may differ from or vary around the requested size.
[335](https://docs.rs#335)///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// ## Callback Size Expectations
[337](https://docs.rs#337)///
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// When you specify [`BufferSize::Fixed(x)`], you are **requesting** that callbacks
[339](https://docs.rs#339)/// receive approximately `x` frames of audio data. However, **no guarantees can be
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// made** about the actual callback size:
[341](https://docs.rs#341)///
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// - The host may round to hardware-supported values
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// - Different devices have different constraints
[344](https://docs.rs#344)/// - The callback size may vary between calls (especially on mobile platforms)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// - The actual size might be larger or smaller than requested
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// ## Latency Considerations
[348](https://docs.rs#348)///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// [`BufferSize::Default`] uses the host's default buffer size, which may be
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// surprisingly large, leading to higher latency. If low latency is desired,
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// [`BufferSize::Fixed`] should be used with a small value in accordance with
[352](https://docs.rs#352)/// the [`SupportedBufferSize`] range from [`SupportedStreamConfig`].
[353](https://docs.rs#353)///
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// Smaller buffer sizes reduce latency but may increase CPU usage and risk audio
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// dropouts if the callback cannot process audio quickly enough.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)///
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// # Example
[358](https://docs.rs#358)///
[359](https://docs.rs#359)/// ```no_run
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
[361](https://docs.rs#361)/// use cpal::{BufferSize, SupportedBufferSize};
[362](https://docs.rs#362)///

[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// # Safety
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    /// The following requirements must be met in order for the safety of `Data`'s API.
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// - The `data` pointer must point to the first sample in the slice containing all samples.
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// - The `len` must describe the length of the buffer as a number of samples in the expected
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    ///   format specified via the `sample_format` argument.
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// - The `sample_format` must correctly represent the underlying sample data delivered/expected
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    ///   by the stream.
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    pub unsafe fn from_parts(data: *mut (), len: usize, sample_format: SampleFormat) -> Self {

[587](https://docs.rs#587)            data,
[588](https://docs.rs#588)            len,
[589](https://docs.rs#589)            sample_format,
[590](https://docs.rs#590)        }
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    }

[602](https://docs.rs#602)    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {

[604](https://docs.rs#604)    }
[605](https://docs.rs#605)
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    /// The raw slice of memory representing the underlying audio data as a slice of bytes.
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    ///
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    /// It is up to the user to interpret the slice of memory based on [`Data::sample_format`].
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    pub fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
[610](https://docs.rs#610)        let len = self.len * self.sample_format.sample_size();
[611](https://docs.rs#611)        // The safety of this block relies on correct construction of the `Data` instance.
[612](https://docs.rs#612)        // See the unsafe `from_parts` constructor for these requirements.
[613](https://docs.rs#613)        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(self.data as *const u8, len) }
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    }
[615](https://docs.rs#615)

[621](https://docs.rs#621)        // The safety of this block relies on correct construction of the `Data` instance. See
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        // the unsafe `from_parts` constructor for these requirements.
[623](https://docs.rs#623)        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(self.data as *mut u8, len) }
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    }

[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// Access the data as a slice of sample type `T`.

[629](https://docs.rs#629)    pub fn as_slice<T>(&self) -> Option<&[T]>

[640](https://docs.rs#640)    }

[701](https://docs.rs#701)    /// Retrieve a [`SupportedStreamConfig`] with the given sample rate.
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    ///
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    /// # Panics
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    ///
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    /// Panics if the given `sample_rate` is outside the range specified within
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    /// this [`SupportedStreamConfigRange`] instance. For a non-panicking
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    /// variant, use [`try_with_sample_rate`](#method.try_with_sample_rate).
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    pub fn with_sample_rate(self, sample_rate: SampleRate) -> SupportedStreamConfig {
[709](https://docs.rs#709)        self.try_with_sample_rate(sample_rate)
[710](https://docs.rs#710)            .expect("sample rate out of range")
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    }
[712](https://docs.rs#712)
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    /// Retrieve a [`SupportedStreamConfig`] with the given sample rate.
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    ///
[715](https://docs.rs#715)    /// Returns `None` if the given sample rate is outside the range specified
[716](https://docs.rs#716)    /// within this [`SupportedStreamConfigRange`] instance.
[717](https://docs.rs#717)    pub fn try_with_sample_rate(self, sample_rate: SampleRate) -> Option<SupportedStreamConfig> {
[718](https://docs.rs#718)        if self.min_sample_rate <= sample_rate && sample_rate <= self.max_sample_rate {
[719](https://docs.rs#719)            Some(SupportedStreamConfig {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)                channels: self.channels,
[721](https://docs.rs#721)                sample_rate,
[722](https://docs.rs#722)                sample_format: self.sample_format,
[723](https://docs.rs#723)                buffer_size: self.buffer_size,
[724](https://docs.rs#724)            })
[725](https://docs.rs#725)        } else {
[726](https://docs.rs#726)            None
[727](https://docs.rs#727)        }
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    }
[729](https://docs.rs#729)

[738](https://docs.rs#738)        }
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    }
[740](https://docs.rs#740)
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// Returns `true` if `rate` falls within `[min_sample_rate, max_sample_rate]`.
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    pub fn contains_rate(&self, rate: SampleRate) -> bool {
[743](https://docs.rs#743)        self.min_sample_rate <= rate && rate <= self.max_sample_rate
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    }
[745](https://docs.rs#745)
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// Retrieve a [`SupportedStreamConfig`] with a standard sample rate.
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    /// The preferred rate is selected in order:
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    /// 1. 48 kHz as the dominant native rate on modern hardware.
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// 2. 44.1 kHz as the standard CD/consumer rate.
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    ///
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    /// Returns `None` if neither standard rate falls within the range specified within this
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// [`SupportedStreamConfigRange`] instance.
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    pub fn try_with_standard_sample_rate(self) -> Option<SupportedStreamConfig> {
[755](https://docs.rs#755)        for rate in [SAMPLE_RATE_48K, SAMPLE_RATE_CD] {
[756](https://docs.rs#756)            if self.contains_rate(rate) {
[757](https://docs.rs#757)                return Some(self.with_sample_rate(rate));
[758](https://docs.rs#758)            }
[759](https://docs.rs#759)        }
[760](https://docs.rs#760)        None
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    }
[762](https://docs.rs#762)
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    /// Retrieve a [`SupportedStreamConfig`] with a standard sample rate.
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    ///
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    /// The preferred rate is selected in order:
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    /// 1. 48 kHz as the dominant native rate on modern hardware.
[767](https://docs.rs#767)    /// 2. 44.1 kHz as the standard CD/consumer rate.
[768](https://docs.rs#768)    ///
[769](https://docs.rs#769)    /// # Panics
[770](https://docs.rs#770)    ///
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    /// Panics if neither standard rate falls within the range specified within this
[772](https://docs.rs#772)    /// [`SupportedStreamConfigRange`] instance. For a non-panicking variant, use
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    /// [`try_with_standard_sample_rate`](Self::try_with_standard_sample_rate).
[774](https://docs.rs#774)    pub fn with_standard_sample_rate(self) -> SupportedStreamConfig {
[775](https://docs.rs#775)        self.try_with_standard_sample_rate()
[776](https://docs.rs#776)            .expect("no standard sample rate (48000 or 44100 Hz) in supported range")
[777](https://docs.rs#777)    }
[778](https://docs.rs#778)
[779](https://docs.rs#779)    /// A comparison function which compares two [`SupportedStreamConfigRange`]s in terms of their
[780](https://docs.rs#780)    /// priority of use as a default stream format.
[781](https://docs.rs#781)    ///
[782](https://docs.rs#782)    /// Some backends do not provide a default stream format for their audio devices. In these
[783](https://docs.rs#783)    /// cases, CPAL attempts to decide on a reasonable default format for the user. To do this we
[784](https://docs.rs#784)    /// use the "greatest" of all supported stream formats when compared with this method.
[785](https://docs.rs#785)    ///
[786](https://docs.rs#786)    /// [`SupportedStreamConfig`]s are prioritised by the following heuristics, applied in order:
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    ///
[788](https://docs.rs#788)    /// **Channels**:
[789](https://docs.rs#789)    ///
[790](https://docs.rs#790)    /// 1. Stereo
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    /// 2. Mono
[792](https://docs.rs#792)    /// 3. Highest available channel count
[793](https://docs.rs#793)    ///
[794](https://docs.rs#794)    /// **Sample format** (most preferred first):
[795](https://docs.rs#795)    ///
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    /// F32 is ranked highest as the universal realtime audio format, followed by F64. Standard
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    /// integer widths descend by bit depth (I32 > I24 > I16); 64-bit integers are deprioritised
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    /// below I16 as accumulator types rather than native stream formats. Signed beats unsigned
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    /// at the same width. DSD ranks last as non-PCM.
[800](https://docs.rs#800)    ///
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    /// **Sample rate**:
[802](https://docs.rs#802)    ///
[803](https://docs.rs#803)    /// 1. 48 kHz (EBU/SMPTE broadcast standard)
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    /// 2. 44.1 kHz (CD standard)
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    /// 3. Highest supported sample rate
[806](https://docs.rs#806)    pub fn cmp_default_heuristics(&self, other: &Self) -> std::cmp::Ordering {
[807](https://docs.rs#807)        use std::cmp::Ordering::Equal;
[808](https://docs.rs#808)
[809](https://docs.rs#809)        let cmp_stereo = (self.channels == 2).cmp(&(other.channels == 2));
[810](https://docs.rs#810)        if cmp_stereo != Equal {
[811](https://docs.rs#811)            return cmp_stereo;
[812](https://docs.rs#812)        }
[813](https://docs.rs#813)
[814](https://docs.rs#814)        let cmp_mono = (self.channels == 1).cmp(&(other.channels == 1));
[815](https://docs.rs#815)        if cmp_mono != Equal {
[816](https://docs.rs#816)            return cmp_mono;
[817](https://docs.rs#817)        }
[818](https://docs.rs#818)
[819](https://docs.rs#819)        let cmp_channels = self.channels.cmp(&other.channels);
[820](https://docs.rs#820)        if cmp_channels != Equal {
[821](https://docs.rs#821)            return cmp_channels;
[822](https://docs.rs#822)        }
[823](https://docs.rs#823)
[824](https://docs.rs#824)        fn format_rank(fmt: SampleFormat) -> u8 {
[825](https://docs.rs#825)            match fmt {
[826](https://docs.rs#826)                SampleFormat::DsdU8 => 0,
[827](https://docs.rs#827)                SampleFormat::DsdU16 => 1,
[828](https://docs.rs#828)                SampleFormat::DsdU32 => 2,
[829](https://docs.rs#829)                SampleFormat::U8 => 3,
[830](https://docs.rs#830)                SampleFormat::I8 => 4,
[831](https://docs.rs#831)                // 64-bit integers: deprioritised below standard audio widths.
[832](https://docs.rs#832)                SampleFormat::U64 => 5,
[833](https://docs.rs#833)                SampleFormat::I64 => 6,
[834](https://docs.rs#834)                SampleFormat::U16 => 7,
[835](https://docs.rs#835)                SampleFormat::I16 => 8,
[836](https://docs.rs#836)                SampleFormat::U24 => 9,
[837](https://docs.rs#837)                SampleFormat::I24 => 10,
[838](https://docs.rs#838)                SampleFormat::U32 => 11,
[839](https://docs.rs#839)                SampleFormat::I32 => 12,
[840](https://docs.rs#840)                SampleFormat::F64 => 13,
[841](https://docs.rs#841)                SampleFormat::F32 => 14,
[842](https://docs.rs#842)            }
[843](https://docs.rs#843)        }
[844](https://docs.rs#844)
[845](https://docs.rs#845)        let cmp_format = format_rank(self.sample_format).cmp(&format_rank(other.sample_format));
[846](https://docs.rs#846)        if cmp_format != Equal {
[847](https://docs.rs#847)            return cmp_format;
[848](https://docs.rs#848)        }
[849](https://docs.rs#849)
[850](https://docs.rs#850)        let cmp_broadcast = self
[851](https://docs.rs#851)            .contains_rate(SAMPLE_RATE_48K)
[852](https://docs.rs#852)            .cmp(&other.contains_rate(SAMPLE_RATE_48K));
[853](https://docs.rs#853)        if cmp_broadcast != Equal {
[854](https://docs.rs#854)            return cmp_broadcast;
[855](https://docs.rs#855)        }
[856](https://docs.rs#856)
[857](https://docs.rs#857)        let cmp_cd = self
[858](https://docs.rs#858)            .contains_rate(SAMPLE_RATE_CD)
[859](https://docs.rs#859)            .cmp(&other.contains_rate(SAMPLE_RATE_CD));
[860](https://docs.rs#860)        if cmp_cd != Equal {
[861](https://docs.rs#861)            return cmp_cd;
[862](https://docs.rs#862)        }
[863](https://docs.rs#863)
[864](https://docs.rs#864)        self.max_sample_rate.cmp(&other.max_sample_rate)
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    }
[866](https://docs.rs#866)}

[874](https://docs.rs#874)#[allow(dead_code)]
[875](https://docs.rs#875)pub(crate) fn validate_stream_config(config: &StreamConfig) -> Result<(), Error> {
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    if config.channels == 0 {
[877](https://docs.rs#877)        return Err(Error::with_message(
[878](https://docs.rs#878)            ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
[879](https://docs.rs#879)            "channel count must be at least 1",
[880](https://docs.rs#880)        ));
[881](https://docs.rs#881)    }
[882](https://docs.rs#882)    if config.sample_rate == 0 {
[883](https://docs.rs#883)        return Err(Error::with_message(
[884](https://docs.rs#884)            ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
[885](https://docs.rs#885)            "sample rate must be at least 1 Hz",
[886](https://docs.rs#886)        ));
[887](https://docs.rs#887)    }
[888](https://docs.rs#888)    if config.buffer_size == BufferSize::Fixed(0) {
[889](https://docs.rs#889)        return Err(Error::with_message(
[890](https://docs.rs#890)            ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
[891](https://docs.rs#891)            "buffer size must be greater than 0",
[892](https://docs.rs#892)        ));
[893](https://docs.rs#893)    }
[894](https://docs.rs#894)    Ok(())
