[994](https://docs.rs#994)    #[test]
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    fn cmp_default_heuristics() {
[996](https://docs.rs#996)        let mut configs = [
[997](https://docs.rs#997)            make_range(1, SampleFormat::F64, 1, 96_000), // mono; loses to all stereo
[998](https://docs.rs#998)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::DsdU8, 1, 96_000), // DSD; lowest format priority
[999](https://docs.rs#999)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::U8, 1, 96_000),
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::I8, 1, 96_000),
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::U16, 1, 96_000),
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::I16, 1, 96_000),
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::F32, 1, 22_050), // neither standard rate
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::F32, 1, 44_100), // 44.1 kHz only
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::F32, 48_000, 96_000), // 48 kHz only
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::F32, 1, 96_000), // both standard rates
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)            make_range(2, SampleFormat::F64, 1, 96_000),
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)        ];
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)        configs.sort_by(|a, b| a.cmp_default_heuristics(b));
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)        // Results in ascending priority order (lowest first):
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)        // [0] Mono loses to every stereo entry regardless of format or rate.
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)        assert_eq!(configs[0].channels(), 1);
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)        assert_eq!(configs[0].sample_format(), SampleFormat::F64);
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)        // [1]–[5] Stereo entries ranked by format (DSD < 8-bit < 16-bit).
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)        assert_eq!(configs[1].sample_format(), SampleFormat::DsdU8);
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)        assert_eq!(configs[2].sample_format(), SampleFormat::U8);
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)        assert_eq!(configs[3].sample_format(), SampleFormat::I8);
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)        assert_eq!(configs[4].sample_format(), SampleFormat::U16);
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)        assert_eq!(configs[5].sample_format(), SampleFormat::I16);
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)        // [6] F64 is outranked by F32.
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)        assert_eq!(configs[6].sample_format(), SampleFormat::F64);
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)        assert_eq!(configs[6].channels(), 2);
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)        // [7]–[10] Stereo F32 entries ranked by rate coverage.
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)        assert_eq!(configs[7].sample_format(), SampleFormat::F32);
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)        assert_eq!(configs[7].max_sample_rate(), 22_050); // neither standard rate
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)        assert_eq!(configs[8].sample_format(), SampleFormat::F32);
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)        assert_eq!(configs[8].max_sample_rate(), 44_100); // 44.1 kHz only
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)        assert_eq!(configs[9].sample_format(), SampleFormat::F32);
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)        assert_eq!(configs[9].min_sample_rate(), 48_000); // 48 kHz only (no 44.1 kHz)
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)        assert_eq!(configs[9].max_sample_rate(), 96_000);
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)        assert_eq!(configs[10].sample_format(), SampleFormat::F32);
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)        assert_eq!(configs[10].min_sample_rate(), 1);
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)        assert_eq!(configs[10].max_sample_rate(), 96_000); // both standard rates
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)    }

}## Expand description

A [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html) provides access to the available audio devices on the system.

Each platform may have a number of available hosts depending on the system, each with their own pros and cons.

For example, WASAPI is the standard audio host API that ships with the Windows operating system. However, due to historical limitations with respect to performance and flexibility, Steinberg created the ASIO API providing better audio device support for pro audio and low-latency applications. As a result, it is common for some devices and device capabilities to only be available via ASIO, while others are only available via WASAPI.

Another great example is the Linux platform. While the ALSA host API is the lowest-level API available to almost all distributions of Linux, its flexibility is limited as it requires that each process have exclusive access to the devices with which they establish streams. PulseAudio is another popular host API that aims to solve this issue by providing user-space mixing, however it has its own limitations w.r.t. low-latency and high-performance audio applications. JACK is yet another host API that is more suitable to pro-audio applications, however it is less readily available by default in many Linux distributions and is known to be tricky to set up.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

An iterator yielding all [ Device](https://docs.rs/trait.DeviceTrait.html)s currently available to the host on the system.

Can be empty if the system does not support audio in general.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `ErrorKind::HostUnavailable`
- `ErrorKind::BackendError`

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

             D: [FnMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnMut.html)(&mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[OutputCallbackInfo](https://docs.rs/struct.OutputCallbackInfo.html)) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + 'static,
             E: [FnMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnMut.html)([Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + 'static { ... }
}## Expand description

A device that is capable of audio input and/or output.

Please note that `Device`s may become invalid if they get disconnected. Therefore, all the
methods that involve a device return a `Result` allowing the user to handle this case.

`try_with_standard_sample_rate`[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/lib.rs.html#806-865)#### pub fn [cmp_default_heuristics](https://docs.rs#method.cmp_default_heuristics)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/lib.rs.html#806-865)

#### pub fn [cmp_default_heuristics](https://docs.rs#method.cmp_default_heuristics)(&self, other: &Self) -> [Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)

A comparison function which compares two [ SupportedStreamConfigRange](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)s in terms of their
priority of use as a default stream format.

Some backends do not provide a default stream format for their audio devices. In these cases, CPAL attempts to decide on a reasonable default format for the user. To do this we use the “greatest” of all supported stream formats when compared with this method.

[ SupportedStreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)s are prioritised by the following heuristics, applied in order:

**Channels**:

- Stereo
- Mono
- Highest available channel count

**Sample format** (most preferred first):

F32 is ranked highest as the universal realtime audio format, followed by F64. Standard integer widths descend by bit depth (I32 > I24 > I16); 64-bit integers are deprioritised below I16 as accumulator types rather than native stream formats. Signed beats unsigned at the same width. DSD ranks last as non-PCM.

**Sample rate**:

- 48 kHz (EBU/SMPTE broadcast standard)
- 44.1 kHz (CD standard)
- Highest supported sample rate

[buffer_size](https://docs.rs#tymethod.buffer_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[FrameCount](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)>;
[now](https://docs.rs#tymethod.now)(&self) -> [StreamInstant](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html);

Start the stream.

Streams returned by `build_*_stream` are always stopped, so `play` must be called before the
data callback will fire. Despite the name, this applies equally to input (capture) streams.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `ErrorKind::DeviceNotAvailable`
- `ErrorKind::StreamInvalidated`

Pause the stream. Some devices support suspending at the hardware level (saving energy); others stop only the data callback while the hardware keeps running.

Note: Not all devices support suspending the stream at the hardware level. This method may fail in these cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-1)Errors

- `ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation`
- `ErrorKind::DeviceNotAvailable`
- `ErrorKind::StreamInvalidated`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/traits.rs.html#469)#### fn [buffer_size](https://docs.rs#tymethod.buffer_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[FrameCount](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/traits.rs.html#469)

#### fn [buffer_size](https://docs.rs#tymethod.buffer_size)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[FrameCount](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)>

Returns the backend’s best available estimate of the number of frames per callback.

The value is available immediately after stream creation: for fixed buffer sizes this is the negotiated hardware size; for default buffer sizes this is the backend’s configured default. The value is updated when it changes during the lifetime of the stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors-2)Errors

- `ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation`
- `ErrorKind::BackendError`

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-notes)Implementation notes

It is not enforced that each callback delivers exactly this many frames. The actual frame count for each callback is given by its buffer.

`buffer_size()` is primarily intended for sizing pre-allocated buffers, but must not be
trusted as a guaranteed bound. An incorrect implementation of `buffer_size()` should not
lead to memory safety violations.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/traits.rs.html#480)#### fn [now](https://docs.rs#tymethod.now)(&self) -> [StreamInstant](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/traits.rs.html#480)

#### fn [now](https://docs.rs#tymethod.now)(&self) -> [StreamInstant](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html)

Returns a [ StreamInstant](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html) representing the current moment on the stream’s clock.

The clock is **monotonic**: successive calls to `now()` will never return a value earlier
than a previous one, and the returned value will never be earlier than any `callback`,
`capture`, or `playback` instant already delivered to the stream’s data callback.

The returned value shares the same time base as the [ StreamInstant](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html)s delivered to the
stream’s data callback via

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.InputStreamTimestamp.html#structfield.callback)

`crate::InputStreamTimestamp::callback`[, so durations between them are meaningful.](https://docs.rs/struct.OutputStreamTimestamp.html#structfield.callback)

`crate::OutputStreamTimestamp::callback`## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Data in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/struct.Data.html

`pub struct Data { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A buffer of dynamically typed audio data, passed to raw stream callbacks.

Raw input stream callbacks receive `&Data`, while raw output stream callbacks expect `&mut Data`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

#### pub unsafe fn [from_parts](https://docs.rs#method.from_parts)(
    data: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html),
    len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    sample_format: [SampleFormat](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html),
) -> Self

Constructor for host implementations to use.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The following requirements must be met in order for the safety of `Data`’s API.

- The `data`pointer must point to the first sample in the slice containing all samples.
- The `len`must describe the length of the buffer as a number of samples in the expected format specified via the`sample_format`argument.
- The `sample_format`must correctly represent the underlying sample data delivered/expected by the stream.

#[non_exhaustive]pub enum DeviceDirection {

## Expand description

The direction(s) that a device supports.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive enums could have additional variants added in future. Therefore, when matching against variants of non-exhaustive enums, an extra wildcard arm must be added to account for any future variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Output)

### Output

## Expand description

Categorization of audio device types.

This describes the kind of audio device (speaker, microphone, headset, etc.) regardless of how it connects to the system.

# HostId in cpal::platform - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/platform/enum.HostId.html

```
pub enum HostId {
    PulseAudio,
    Jack,
    Alsa,
    Custom,
}
```
**DragonFly BSD or FreeBSD or Linux or NetBSD**only.

## Expand description

Unique identifier for available hosts on the platform.

Only the hosts supported by the current platform are available as enum variants.
For cross-platform code that needs to handle hosts from other platforms,
use the string representation via [ std::fmt::Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)/

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html)

`std::str::FromStr`[§](https://docs.rs#available-host-strings)Available Host Strings

For cross-platform matching, these host strings are available:

- `"aaudio"`- Android Audio
- `"alsa"`- Advanced Linux Sound Architecture
- `"asio"`- ASIO
- `"audioworklet"`- Audio Worklet
- `"coreaudio"`- CoreAudio
- `"custom"`- Custom host (requires- `custom`feature)
- `"jack"`- JACK Audio Connection Kit
- `"null"`- Null host
- `"wasapi"`- Windows Audio Session API
- `"webaudio"`- Web Audio API

[§](https://docs.rs#cross-platform-example)Cross-Platform Example

```
use cpal::HostId;
use std::str::FromStr;
fn handle_host_string(host_string: &str) {
    // String matching works on all platforms
    match host_string {
        "alsa" => println!("ALSA host"),
        "coreaudio" => println!("CoreAudio host"),
        "jack" => println!("JACK host"),
        "wasapi" => println!("WASAPI host"),
        "asio" => println!("ASIO host"),
        "aaudio" => println!("AAudio host"),
        _ => println!("Other host"),
    }
    // Parse host string (may fail if host is not available on this platform)
    if let Ok(host_id) = HostId::from_str(host_string) {
        println!("Successfully parsed: {}", host_id);
    }
}
```

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/platform/mod.rs.html#824-830)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-HostId)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/platform/mod.rs.html#824-830)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Eq-for-HostId)

Parse a host identifier from its string representation (e.g. `"alsa"`,
`"coreaudio"`).

The comparison is case-insensitive. Only hosts compiled in for the current platform are recognized; a host string that is valid on another platform is still an error here.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation`

# assert_stream_send in cpal - Rust

macro_rules! assert_stream_send {
    ($t:ty) => { ... };
}

## Expand description

can be safely transferred between threads, as required by CPAL’s API.

use cpal::assert_stream_send;

```

# DeviceId in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/struct.DeviceId.html

`pub struct DeviceId(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A stable identifier for an audio device across all supported platforms.

Device IDs should remain stable across application restarts and can be serialized using `Display`/`FromStr`.

A device ID consists of a [ HostId](https://docs.rs/platform/enum.HostId.html) identifying the audio backend and a device-specific identifier string.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use cpal::traits::{HostTrait, DeviceTrait};
use cpal::DeviceId;
use std::str::FromStr;
let host = cpal::default_host();
let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
let device_id = device.id().unwrap();
// Serialize to string (e.g., for storage in config file)
let id_string = device_id.to_string();
println!("Device ID: {}", id_string); // e.g., "wasapi:device_identifier"
// Deserialize from string
match DeviceId::from_str(&id_string) {
    Ok(parsed_id) => {
        // Retrieve the device by its ID
        if let Some(device) = host.device_by_id(&parsed_id) {
            println!("Found device: {:?}", device.id());
        }
    }
    Err(e) => eprintln!("Failed to parse device ID: {}", e),
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a `DeviceId` from a host identifier and a device-specific identifier string.

This constructor is used by backend implementations. Application code should obtain
`DeviceId` values through [ DeviceTrait::id](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.id) and persist them via

[/](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html)

`FromStr`## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cpal/lib.rs.html#267)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Eq-for-DeviceId)

Parse a device identifier from its string representation (e.g. `"alsa:hw:0,0"`).

The format is `"<host>:<device>"` where `<host>` is the lowercase host name (see
[ HostId](https://docs.rs/platform/enum.HostId.html)) and

`<device>` is the device-specific identifier string.[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

- `ErrorKind::InvalidInput`- `"host:device"`format.
- `ErrorKind::UnsupportedOperation`

# I24 in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/struct.I24.html

`pub struct I24(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

24-bit signed integer sample type.

Represents 24-bit audio with range `-(1 << 23)..=((1 << 23) - 1)`.

**Note:** While representing 24-bit audio, this format uses 4 bytes (i32) of storage
with the most significant byte unused. Use [ SampleFormat::bits_per_sample](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html#method.bits_per_sample) to get
the actual bit depth (24) vs

[for storage size (4 bytes).](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html#method.sample_size)

`SampleFormat::sample_size`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct a new sample if the given value is within range.

Returns `None` if `val` is out of range.

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/types.rs.html#251-252)#### pub fn [new_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.new_unchecked)(s: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)) -> [I24](https://docs.rs/struct.I24.html)

Constructs a new sample without checking for overflowing.

This should *only* be used if the user can guarantee the sample will be within
range and they require the extra performance.

If this function is used, the sample crate can’t guarantee that the returned sample or any interacting samples will remain within their MIN and MAX bounds.

# StreamInstant in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/struct.StreamInstant.html

`pub struct StreamInstant { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A monotonic time instance associated with a stream, retrieved from either:

- A timestamp provided to the stream’s underlying audio data callback or
- The same time source used to generate timestamps for a stream’s underlying audio data callback.

`StreamInstant` represents a moment on a stream’s monotonic clock. Because the underlying clock
is monotonic, `StreamInstant` values are always positive and increasing.

Within a single stream, all instants share the same clock, so arithmetic between them is meaningful. Across different streams, origins are not guaranteed to be shared. On some hosts each stream starts its own independent clock at zero, so subtracting a timestamp from one stream and one from another may produce a meaningless result.

[§](https://docs.rs#time-sources-by-host)Time sources by host

| Host | Time source |
|---|---|
| AAudio | `AAudioStream_getTimestamp(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` |
| ALSA | `snd_pcm_status_get_htstamp()` |
| ASIO | `timeGetTime()` |
| AudioWorklet | `AudioContext.currentTime` |
| CoreAudio | `mach_absolute_time()` |
| JACK | `jack_get_time()` |
| PipeWire | `pw_stream_get_time_n()` |
| PulseAudio | `std::time::Instant` |
| WASAPI | `QueryPerformanceCounter()` |
| WebAudio | `AudioContext.currentTime` |

Disclaimer:These system calls might change over time.

Note:The`+`and`-`operators on`StreamInstant`may panic if the result cannot be represented as a`StreamInstant`. Use[or](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html#method.checked_add)`checked_add`[for non-panicking variants.](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamInstant.html#method.checked_sub)`checked_sub`

# U24 in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/struct.U24.html

`pub struct U24(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

24-bit unsigned integer sample type.

Represents 24-bit audio with range `0..=((1 << 24) - 1)`, with origin at `1 << 23 == 8388608`.

**Note:** While representing 24-bit audio, this format uses 4 bytes (u32) of storage
with the most significant byte unused. Use [ SampleFormat::bits_per_sample](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html#method.bits_per_sample) to get
the actual bit depth (24) vs

[for storage size (4 bytes).](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html#method.sample_size)

`SampleFormat::sample_size`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct a new sample if the given value is within range.

Returns `None` if `val` is out of range.

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/types.rs.html#276-277)#### pub fn [new_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.new_unchecked)(s: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)) -> [U24](https://docs.rs/struct.U24.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/types.rs.html#276-277)

#### pub fn [new_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.new_unchecked)(s: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)) -> [U24](https://docs.rs/struct.U24.html)

Constructs a new sample without checking for overflowing.

This should *only* be used if the user can guarantee the sample will be within
range and they require the extra performance.

If this function is used, the sample crate can’t guarantee that the returned sample or any interacting samples will remain within their MIN and MAX bounds.

# BufferSize in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/enum.BufferSize.html

```
pub enum BufferSize {
    Default,
    Fixed(
```
[FrameCount](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html)),
}## Expand description

The buffer size requests the callback size for audio streams.

This controls the approximate size of the audio buffer passed to your callback. The actual callback size depends on the host/platform implementation and hardware constraints, and may differ from or vary around the requested size.

[§](https://docs.rs#callback-size-expectations)Callback Size Expectations

When you specify [ BufferSize::Fixed(x)](https://docs.rs/enum.BufferSize.html#variant.Fixed), you are

**requesting**that callbacks receive approximately

`x` frames of audio data. However, **no guarantees can be made**about the actual callback size:

- The host may round to hardware-supported values
- Different devices have different constraints
- The callback size may vary between calls (especially on mobile platforms)
- The actual size might be larger or smaller than requested

[§](https://docs.rs#latency-considerations)Latency Considerations

[ BufferSize::Default](https://docs.rs/enum.BufferSize.html#variant.Default) uses the host’s default buffer size, which may be
surprisingly large, leading to higher latency. If low latency is desired,

[should be used with a small value in accordance with the](https://docs.rs/enum.BufferSize.html#variant.Fixed)

`BufferSize::Fixed`[range from](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html#method.buffer_size)

`SupportedBufferSize`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`Smaller buffer sizes reduce latency but may increase CPU usage and risk audio dropouts if the callback cannot process audio quickly enough.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
use cpal::{BufferSize, SupportedBufferSize};
let host = cpal::default_host();
let device = host.default_output_device().unwrap();
let config = device.default_output_config().unwrap();
// Check supported buffer size range
match config.buffer_size() {
    SupportedBufferSize::Range { min, max } => {
        println!("Buffer size range: {} - {}", min, max);
        // Request a small buffer for low latency
        let mut stream_config = config.config();
        stream_config.buffer_size = BufferSize::Fixed(256);
    }
    SupportedBufferSize::Unknown => {
        // Platform doesn't expose buffer size control
        println!("Buffer size cannot be queried on this platform");
    }
}
```

# ErrorKind in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/enum.ErrorKind.html

#[non_exhaustive]pub enum ErrorKind {
```
## Show 14 variants

    DeviceBusy,
    DeviceChanged,
    DeviceNotAvailable,
    HostUnavailable,
    InvalidInput,
    PermissionDenied,
    RealtimeDenied,
    ResourceExhausted,
    StreamInvalidated,
    UnsupportedConfig,
    UnsupportedOperation,
    Xrun,
    BackendError,
    Other,
}## Expand description

A list specifying general categories of CPAL error.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DeviceBusy)

### DeviceBusy

The device is temporarily busy. This can happen when another application or stream is using the device. Retrying after a short delay may succeed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DeviceChanged)

### DeviceChanged

The active audio route changed and the stream was automatically rerouted. The stream remains active and no rebuild is required.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DeviceNotAvailable)

### DeviceNotAvailable

The requested audio device is not available.

This can happen if the device has been disconnected while the program is running, or if the device identifier refers to a device that does not exist on this system.

The audio host (server or subsystem) is not available on this system.

This is distinct from [ DeviceNotAvailable](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.DeviceNotAvailable): when a host (e.g. PulseAudio, PipeWire, JACK,
or kernel subsystem) is absent or not running, no devices can be reached through it.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidInput)

### InvalidInput

Invalid input or argument.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PermissionDenied)

### PermissionDenied

Access to the device or resource was denied by the operating system or audio subsystem.

The device exists and may be functional, but the current process or user does not have permission to use it. Common causes include microphone privacy settings (iOS, macOS), missing audio group membership (Linux), or file permission errors.

Unlike [ DeviceNotAvailable](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.DeviceNotAvailable), which signals absence, this variant signals an
authorization failure.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RealtimeDenied)

### RealtimeDenied

A real-time scheduling promotion or equivalent platform performance mode was refused. Audio will still play, but may be subject to increased latency or glitches under load.

Absence of this error does **not** mean real-time quality is active: the check may not
have been attempted (feature flag disabled, device ineligible, or the host manages
scheduling internally).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ResourceExhausted)

### ResourceExhausted

An OS resource limit was reached, such as a system or process thread or memory limit.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.StreamInvalidated)

### StreamInvalidated

The stream configuration is no longer valid and must be rebuilt.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UnsupportedConfig)

### UnsupportedConfig

The requested stream configuration is not supported. This includes unsupported sample rates, channel counts, or sample formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UnsupportedOperation)

### UnsupportedOperation

The requested operation is not supported. This includes unsupported stream directions (e.g., requesting input on an output-only device), unavailable features, or operations not implemented by the backend.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Xrun)

### Xrun

A buffer underrun or overrun occurred, causing a potential audio glitch.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.BackendError)

### BackendError

The underlying platform audio API returned an error that CPAL cannot map to a more specific error kind.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Other)

### Other

A catch-all for errors that do not fall under any other CPAL error kind.

CPAL itself emits this variant only for genuinely unclassifiable conditions. Treat them as permanent: no retry strategy is possible without host-specific knowledge.

New [ ErrorKind](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html) variants may be added in future releases to cover specific cases
currently reported as

`Other`.## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# SampleFormat in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/enum.SampleFormat.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum SampleFormat {
```
## Show 15 variants

    I8,
    I16,
    I24,
    I32,
    I64,
    U8,
    U16,
    U24,
    U32,
    U64,
    F32,
    F64,
    DsdU8,
    DsdU16,
    DsdU32,
}## Expand description

Format that each sample has. Usually, this corresponds to the sampling
depth of the audio source. For example, 16 bit quantized samples can be
encoded in `i16` or `u16`. Note that the quantized sampling depth is not
directly visible for formats where [ is_float](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html#method.is_float) is true.

Also note that the backend must support the encoding of the quantized
samples in the given format, as there is no generic transformation from one
format into the other done inside the frontend-library code. You can query
the supported formats by using [ supported_input_configs](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs).

A good rule of thumb is to use [ SampleFormat::I16](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html#variant.I16) as this covers typical
music (WAV, MP3) as well as typical audio input devices on most platforms,

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I8)

### I8

`i8` with a valid range of `i8::MIN..=i8::MAX` with `0` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I16)

### I16

`i16` with a valid range of `i16::MIN..=i16::MAX` with `0` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I24)

### I24

`I24` with a valid range of `-(1 << 23)..=((1 << 23) - 1)` with `0` being the origin.

This format uses 4 bytes of storage but only 24 bits are significant.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I32)

### I32

`i32` with a valid range of `i32::MIN..=i32::MAX` with `0` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.I64)

### I64

`i64` with a valid range of `i64::MIN..=i64::MAX` with `0` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.U8)

### U8

`u8` with a valid range of `u8::MIN..=u8::MAX` with `1 << 7 == 128` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.U16)

### U16

`u16` with a valid range of `u16::MIN..=u16::MAX` with `1 << 15 == 32768` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.U24)

### U24

`U24` with a valid range of `0..=((1 << 24) - 1)` with `1 << 23 == 8388608` being the origin.

This format uses 4 bytes of storage but only 24 bits are significant.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.U32)

### U32

`u32` with a valid range of `u32::MIN..=u32::MAX` with `1 << 31` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.U64)

### U64

`U48` with a valid range of ‘0..(1 << 48)’ with `1 << 47` being the origin
`u64` with a valid range of `u64::MIN..=u64::MAX` with `1 << 63` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.F32)

### F32

`f32` with a valid range of `-1.0..=1.0` with `0.0` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.F64)

### F64

`f64` with a valid range of `-1.0..=1.0` with `0.0` being the origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DsdU8)

### DsdU8

DSD 1-bit stream in u8 container (8 bits = 8 DSD samples) with 0x69 being the silence byte pattern.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DsdU16)

### DsdU16

DSD 1-bit stream in u16 container (16 bits = 16 DSD samples) with 0x69 being the silence byte pattern.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DsdU32)

### DsdU32

DSD 1-bit stream in u32 container (32 bits = 32 DSD samples) with 0x69 being the silence byte pattern.

# FromSample in cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/0.18.1/cpal/trait.FromSample.html

```
pub trait FromSample<S> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[from_sample_](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_sample_)(s: S) -> Self;
}## Expand description

Similar to the std `From` trait, but specifically for converting between sample types.

We use this trait to be generic over the `Sample::to_sample` and `Sample::from_sample` methods.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

}## Expand description

A trait for working generically across different **Sample** format types.

Provides methods for converting to and from any type that implements the
[ FromSample](https://docs.rs/trait.FromSample.html) trait and provides methods for performing signal
amplitude addition and multiplication.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use dasp_sample::{I24, Sample};
fn main() {
    assert_eq!((-1.0).to_sample::<u8>(), 0);
    assert_eq!(0.0.to_sample::<u8>(), 128);
    assert_eq!(0i32.to_sample::<u32>(), 2_147_483_648);
    assert_eq!(I24::new(0).unwrap(), Sample::from_sample(0.0));
    assert_eq!(0.0, Sample::EQUILIBRIUM);
}
```
## Required Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-consts)

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/lib.rs.html#86)#### const [EQUILIBRIUM](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.EQUILIBRIUM): Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/lib.rs.html#86)

#### const [EQUILIBRIUM](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.EQUILIBRIUM): Self

The equilibrium value for the wave that this `Sample` type represents. This is normally the
value that is equal distance from both the min and max ranges of the sample.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use dasp_sample::Sample;
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(0.0, f32::EQUILIBRIUM);
    assert_eq!(0, i32::EQUILIBRIUM);
    assert_eq!(128, u8::EQUILIBRIUM);
    assert_eq!(32_768_u16, Sample::EQUILIBRIUM);
}
```
**Note:** This will likely be changed to an “associated const” if the feature lands.

## Provided Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#provided-associated-consts)

The multiplicative identity of the signal.

In other words: A value which when used to scale/multiply the amplitude or frequency of a signal, returns the same signal.

This is useful as a default, non-affecting amplitude or frequency multiplier.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use dasp_sample::{Sample, U48};
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(1.0, f32::IDENTITY);
    assert_eq!(1.0, i8::IDENTITY);
    assert_eq!(1.0, u8::IDENTITY);
    assert_eq!(1.0, U48::IDENTITY);
}
```
## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

#### type [Signed](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Signed): [SignedSample](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/trait.SignedSample.html) + [Duplex](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/conv/trait.Duplex.html)<Self>

When summing two samples of a signal together, it is necessary for both samples to be
represented in some signed format. This associated `Addition` type represents the format to
which `Self` should be converted for optimal `Addition` performance.

For example, u32’s optimal `Addition` type would be i32, u8’s would be i8, f32’s would be
f32, etc.

Specifying this as an associated type allows us to automatically determine the optimal,
lossless Addition format type for summing any two unique `Sample` types together.

As a user of the `sample` crate, you will never need to be concerned with this type unless
you are defining your own unique `Sample` type(s).

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/lib.rs.html#67)#### type [Float](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Float): [FloatSample](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/trait.FloatSample.html) + [Duplex](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/conv/trait.Duplex.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/lib.rs.html#67)

#### type [Float](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Float): [FloatSample](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/trait.FloatSample.html) + [Duplex](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dasp_sample/conv/trait.Duplex.html)<Self>

When multiplying two samples of a signal together, it is necessary for both samples to be
represented in some signed, floating-point format. This associated `Multiplication` type
represents the format to which `Self` should be converted for optimal `Multiplication`
performance.

For example, u32’s optimal `Multiplication` type would be f32, u64’s would be f64, i8’s
would be f32, etc.

Specifying this as an associated type allows us to automatically determine the optimal,
lossless Multiplication format type for multiplying any two unique `Sample` types together.

As a user of the `sample` crate, you will never need to be concerned with this type unless
you are defining your own unique `Sample` type(s).

[Source](https://docs.rs/dasp_sample/0.11.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/dasp_sample/lib.rs.html#188)

#### fn [to_float_sample](https://docs.rs#method.to_float_sample)(self) -> Self::[Float](https://docs.rs/trait.Sample.html#associatedtype.Float)

Converts `self` to the equivalent `Sample` in the associated `Float` format.

This is a simple wrapper around `Sample::to_sample` which may provide extra convenience in
some cases, particularly for assisting type inference.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use dasp_sample::Sample;
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(128_u8.to_float_sample(), 0.0);
}
```
Adds (or “offsets”) the amplitude of the `Sample` by the given signed amplitude.

`Self` will be converted to `Self::Signed`, the addition will occur and then the result
will be converted back to `Self`. These conversions allow us to correctly handle the
addition of unsigned signal formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
use dasp_sample::Sample;
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(0.25.add_amp(0.5), 0.75);
    assert_eq!(192u8.add_amp(-128), 64);
}
```
Multiplies (or “scales”) the amplitude of the `Sample` by the given float amplitude.

- `amp`> 1.0 amplifies the sample.
- `amp`< 1.0 attenuates the sample.
- `amp`== 1.0 yields the same sample.
- `amp`== 0.0 yields the- `Sample::EQUILIBRIUM`.

`Self` will be converted to `Self::Float`, the multiplication will occur and then the
result will be converted back to `Self`. These conversions allow us to correctly handle the
multiplication of integral signal formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
use dasp_sample::Sample;
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(64_i8.mul_amp(0.5), 32);
    assert_eq!(0.5.mul_amp(-2.0), -1.0);
    assert_eq!(64_u8.mul_amp(0.0), 128);
}
```

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/cpal/

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/latest/aarch64-apple-ios/cpal/

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```

use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};

    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/latest/wasm32-unknown-unknown/cpal/

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescription](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescription.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescriptionBuilder](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescriptionBuilder.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDirection](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceDirection.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceType.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [InterfaceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.InterfaceType.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [available_hosts](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.available_hosts.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html);
- `pub use platform::`- [host_from_id](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.host_from_id.html);

# cpal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpal/latest/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/cpal/

## Expand description

Low-level library for audio input and output, written in Rust.

For higher-level audio playback and capture, consider
[Rodio](https://github.com/RustAudio/rodio) or similar libraries.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-cpal)How to use cpal

Here are some concepts cpal exposes:

- A `Host`[default_host](https://docs.rs/platform/fn.default_host.html)that is guaranteed to be available.
- A `Device`
- A `Stream`[Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html)will run your stream before you can create one. Often, a default device can be retrieved via the[Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html).

The first step is to initialise the [ Host](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Host.html):

```
use cpal::traits::HostTrait;
let host = cpal::default_host();
```
Then choose an available [ Device](https://docs.rs/platform/struct.Device.html). The easiest way is to use the default input or output

`Device` via the [or](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_input_device)

`default_input_device()`[methods on](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.default_output_device)

`default_output_device()``host`.Alternatively, you can enumerate all the available devices with the [ devices()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.HostTrait.html#tymethod.devices) method.
Beware that the

`default_*_device()` functions return an `Option<Device>` in case no device
is available for that stream type on the system.`let device = host.default_output_device().expect("no output device available");`Before we can create a stream, we must decide what the configuration of the audio stream is
going to be.
You can query all the supported configurations with the
[ supported_input_configs()](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_input_configs) and

[methods. These produce a list of](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.DeviceTrait.html#tymethod.supported_output_configs)

`supported_output_configs()`[structs which can later be turned into actual](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfigRange.html)

`SupportedStreamConfigRange`[structs.](https://docs.rs/struct.SupportedStreamConfig.html)

`SupportedStreamConfig`If you don’t want to query the list of configs,
you can also build your own [ StreamConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamConfig.html) manually, but doing so could lead to an error when
building the stream if the config is not supported by the device.

Note: the`supported_input/output_configs()`methods could return an error for example if the device has been disconnected.

```
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait};
let mut supported_configs_range = device.supported_output_configs()
    .expect("error while querying configs");
let supported_config = supported_configs_range.next()
    .expect("no supported config?!")
    .with_max_sample_rate();
```
Now that we have everything for the stream, we are ready to create it from our selected device:

```
use cpal::Data;
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let stream = device.build_output_stream(
    config,
    move |data: &mut [f32], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo| {
        // react to stream events and read or write stream data here.
    },
    move |err| {
        // react to errors here.
    },
    None // Timeout for stream initialization: None = wait indefinitely,
         // Some(Duration) = time to wait for the backend to initialize the stream.
);
```
Streams are returned in a paused state. Once the stream has been started with
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play), the selected audio device will periodically call
the data callback that was passed to the function. For input streams, the callback receives

`&`[containing captured audio samples. For output streams, the callback receives](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data``&mut`[to be filled with audio samples for playback.](https://docs.rs/struct.Data.html)

`Data`

Note: Creating and running a stream willnotblock the thread. On modern platforms, the given callback is called by a dedicated, high-priority thread responsible for delivering audio data to the system’s audio device in a timely manner. On older platforms that only provide a blocking API (e.g. ALSA), CPAL will create a thread in order to consistently provide non-blocking behaviour (currently this is a thread per stream, but this may change to use a single thread for all streams).If this is an issue for your platform or design, please share your issue and use-case with the CPAL team on the GitHub issue tracker for consideration.

In this example, we simply fill the given output buffer with silence.

```
use cpal::{Data, Sample, SampleFormat, FromSample};
use cpal::traits::{DeviceTrait, HostTrait, StreamTrait};
let err_fn = |err| eprintln!("an error occurred on the output audio stream: {}", err);
let sample_format = supported_config.sample_format();
let config = supported_config.into();
let stream = match sample_format {
    SampleFormat::F32 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<f32>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::I16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<i16>, err_fn, None),
    SampleFormat::U16 => device.build_output_stream(config, write_silence::<u16>, err_fn, None),
    sample_format => panic!("Unsupported sample format '{sample_format}'")
}.unwrap();
fn write_silence<T: Sample>(data: &mut [T], _: &cpal::OutputCallbackInfo) {
    for sample in data.iter_mut() {
        *sample = Sample::EQUILIBRIUM;
    }
}
```
Streams are always returned in a paused state, so we must call
[ Stream::play](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.StreamTrait.html#tymethod.play) to start running the data callback.

`stream.play().unwrap();`Some devices support pausing the audio stream. This can be useful for saving energy in moments of silence.

`stream.pause().unwrap();`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescription](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescription.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDescriptionBuilder](https://docs.rs/device_description/struct.DeviceDescriptionBuilder.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceDirection](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceDirection.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [DeviceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.DeviceType.html);
- `pub use device_description::`- [InterfaceType](https://docs.rs/device_description/enum.InterfaceType.html);

- [Sample](https://docs.rs/enum.SampleFormat.html)- Format
- Format that each sample has. Usually, this corresponds to the sampling
depth of the audio source. For example, 16 bit quantized samples can be
encoded in `i16`or`u16`. Note that the quantized sampling depth is not directly visible for formats where`is_float`
- [Supported](https://docs.rs/enum.SupportedBufferSize.html)- Buffer - Size
- Describes the minimum and maximum supported buffer size for the device

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [SAMPLE_](https://docs.rs/constant.SAMPLE_RATE_48K.html)- RATE_ - 48K
- 48 kHz: the EBU/SMPTE broadcast standard, default on most modern hardware.
- [SAMPLE_](https://docs.rs/constant.SAMPLE_RATE_CD.html)- RATE_ - CD
- 44.1 kHz: the CD standard, widely used in music production and consumer audio.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromSample.html)- Sample
- Similar to the std `From`trait, but specifically for converting between sample types.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/trait.Sample.html)
- A trait for working generically across different **Sample**format types.
- [Sized](https://docs.rs/trait.SizedSample.html)- Sample
- A `Sample``SampleFormat`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Channel](https://docs.rs/type.ChannelCount.html)- Count
- Number of channels.
- [Devices](https://docs.rs/type.DevicesFiltered.html)- Filtered
- Iterator of devices wrapped in a filter to only include certain device types
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/type.FrameCount.html)- Count
- A frame represents one sample for each channel. For example, with stereo audio, one frame contains two samples (left and right channels).
- [Input](https://docs.rs/type.InputDevices.html)- Devices
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *input*devices.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/type.OutputDevices.html)- Devices
- A host’s device iterator yielding only *output*devices.
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/type.SampleRate.html)- Rate
- The number of samples processed per second for a single channel of audio.

# anyhow 1.0.103 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anyhow/^1.0

# Anyhow ¯\_(°ペ)_/¯

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0/anyhow/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error type
for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use Result;`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like "No such file or directory" can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use ;``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use Error;`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err;`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!;`

## No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled "std" feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow's error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Comparison to failure

The `anyhow::Error` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library's `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

## Comparison to thiserror

Use Anyhow if you don't care what error type your functions return, you just
want it to be easy. This is common in application code. Use [thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror) if you
are a library that wants to design your own dedicated error type(s) so that on
failures the caller gets exactly the information that you choose.

# Hound

A wav encoding and decoding library in Rust.

Hound can read and write the WAVE audio format, an ubiquitous format for raw,
uncompressed audio. The main motivation to write it was to test
[Claxon](https://github.com/ruuda/claxon), a FLAC decoding library written in Rust.

## Examples

The following example renders a 440 Hz sine wave, and stores it as a mono wav file with a sample rate of 44.1 kHz and 16 bits per sample.

```
use PI;
use i16;
use hound;
let spec = WavSpec ;
let mut writer = create.unwrap;
for t in .map
```
The file is finalized implicitly when the writer is dropped, call
`writer.finalize()` to observe errors.

The following example computes the root mean square (RMS) of an audio file with at most 16 bits per sample.

```
use hound;
let mut reader = open.unwrap;
let sqr_sum = reader.
                    .fold;
println!;
```
## Features

| Read | Write | |
|---|---|---|
| Format | `PCMWAVEFORMAT`,`WAVEFORMATEX`,`WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE` | `PCMWAVEFORMAT`,`WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE` |
| Encoding | Integer PCM, IEEE Float | Integer PCM, IEEE Float |
| Bits per sample | 8, 16, 24, 32 (integer), 32 (float) | 8, 16, 24, 32 (integer), 32 (float) |

# ringbuf 0.4.8 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ringbuf/^0.4

# ringbuf

Lock-free SPSC FIFO ring buffer with direct access to inner data.

## Features

- Lock-free operations - they succeed or fail immediately without blocking or waiting.
- Arbitrary item type (not only `Copy`).
- Items can be inserted and removed one by one or many at once.
- Thread-safe direct access to the internal ring buffer memory.
- `Read`and- `Write`implementation.
- Overwriting insertion support.
- Different types of buffers and underlying storages.
- Can be used without `std`and even without`alloc`(using only statically-allocated memory).
- Async and blocking versions (see [this section](https://docs.rs#derived-crates)).
- Can optionally use the `portable-atomic`

# Usage

At first you need to create the ring buffer itself. `HeapRb` is recommended but you may [choose another one](https://docs.rs#types).

After the ring buffer is created it may be splitted into pair of `Producer` and `Consumer`.
Producer is used to insert items to the ring buffer, consumer - to remove items from it.

# Types

There are several types of ring buffers provided:

- `LocalRb`. Only for single-threaded use.
- `SharedRb`. Can be shared between threads. Its frequently used instances:- `HeapRb`. Contents are stored in dynamic memory.- *Recommended for use in most cases.*
- `StaticRb`. Contents can be stored in statically-allocated memory.

You may also provide your own generic parameters.

# Performance

`SharedRb` needs to synchronize CPU cache between CPU cores. This synchronization has some overhead.
To avoid multiple unnecessary synchronizations you may use methods that operate many items at once
(`push_slice`/`push_iter`, `pop_slice`/`pop_iter`, etc.)
or you can `freeze` producer or consumer and then synchronize threads manually (see items in `frozen` module).

For single-threaded usage `LocalRb` is recommended because it is slightly faster than `SharedRb` due to absence of CPU cache synchronization.

## Examples

### Simple

```
use ;
let rb = new;
let  = rb.split;
prod.try_push.unwrap;
prod.try_push.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
prod.try_push.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
### No heap

```
use ;
const RB_SIZE: usize = 1;
let mut rb = default;
let  = rb.split_ref;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Overwrite

Ring buffer can be used in overwriting mode when insertion overwrites the latest element if the buffer is full.

```
use ;
let mut rb = new;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Note that `push_overwrite` requires exclusive access to the ring buffer
so to perform it concurrently you need to guard the ring buffer with mutex or some other lock.

# wasm-bindgen 0.2.126 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen/^0.2

Built with 🦀🕸 by The Rust and WebAssembly Working Group

## Install `wasm-bindgen-cli`

You can install it using `cargo install`:

```
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli
```
Or, you can download it from the
[release page](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/releases).

If you have [ cargo-binstall](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-binstall) installed,
then you can install the pre-built artifacts by running:

```
cargo binstall wasm-bindgen-cli
```
## Example

Import JavaScript things into Rust and export Rust things to JavaScript.

```
use *;
// Import the `window.alert` function from the Web.
extern "C"
// Export a `greet` function from Rust to JavaScript, that alerts a
// hello message.
```
Use exported Rust things from JavaScript with ECMAScript modules!

```
import  from "./hello_world";
;
```
## Features

-
**Lightweight.**Only pay for what you use.`wasm-bindgen`only generates bindings and glue for the JavaScript imports you actually use and Rust functionality that you export. For example, importing and using the`document.querySelector`method doesn't cause`Node.prototype.appendChild`or`window.alert`to be included in the bindings as well.
-
**ECMAScript modules.**Just import WebAssembly modules the same way you would import JavaScript modules. Future compatible with[WebAssembly modules and ECMAScript modules integration](https://github.com/WebAssembly/esm-integration).
-
**Designed with the**Eventually, there won't be any JavaScript shims between Rust-generated wasm functions and native DOM methods. Because the Wasm functions are statically type checked, some of those native methods' dynamic type checks should become unnecessary, promising to unlock even-faster-than-JavaScript DOM access.["Web IDL bindings" proposal](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals/issues/8)in mind.

`wasm-bindgen-futures`

This crate bridges the gap between Rust `Future`s and JavaScript `Promise`s.

As of this version the implementation lives in [ js-sys](https://docs.rs/js-sys) under the

`futures`
feature. Depending on this crate automatically activates that feature, which

use Promise;

async
```

- `future_to_promise_typed`- `future_to_promise`

Under the feature flag `futures-core-03-stream` there is support for
`AsyncIterator` to `Stream` conversion via `JsStream`.
